Consensus on where a release ends: finding the resting scenes of a mug and a spoon

Abstract. We propose a way to find the families of resting scenes of a mug and a spoon on a table, from the spoon lying beside the mug to the spoon standing inside it, starting from random placements only. Particles of polarised consensus-based optimisation search a space of touching scenes, in which each body is lowered until it touches. Both the objective and the distance between particles are taken from a one-second simulated release: a particle is scored by how far the release carries its scene, and two particles count as near only if their scenes start near each other and end near each other.

1. Choosing the search space

We want to arrange a mug and a spoon on a table so that, when released, they stay where they are. There can be many families of such arrangements: the spoon can lie beside the mug, lean against it, rest across its rim or stand inside it. The aim is to keep scenes from as many families as possible in one population of particles.

To describe one arrangement, first fix a coordinate system to each body. A point \(p\in\mathbb R^3\) then identifies the same material point of that body wherever it is placed. Its position in the world is determined by a rotation matrix \(R_b\) and a translation vector \(t_b\), where \(b\) denotes the mug or the spoon. The rotation changes the direction of the body's axes; the translation gives the world position of its coordinate origin. Rotation matrices satisfy

$$SO(3)=\{R\in\mathbb R^{3\times3}:R^\top R=I_3,\ \det R=1\},$$

where \(I_3\) is the three-dimensional identity matrix. A body's pose is the pair \(g_b=(R_b,t_b)\), and a scene \(s\) consists of both poses:

$$s=\bigl((R_{\text{mug}},t_{\text{mug}}),(R_{\text{spoon}},t_{\text{spoon}})\bigr).$$

We can now write the world position of the material point \(p\) in that scene as

$$y_b(p;s)=R_bp+t_b.$$

This relation will be used both to construct scenes and to compare how much their bodies move. The table is the plane \(z=0\). Moving the entire scene horizontally, or turning it as a whole about the vertical, leaves the physical problem unchanged. We remove this freedom by placing the mug's centre of mass above the horizontal origin and choosing a fixed reference for its heading. This choice is the table gauge; it leaves the mug's tilt and the spoon's position and orientation relative to the mug free.

We could search directly over the two poses, including the height of each body. Many trial scenes would then have bodies hovering above the table, and their release would mostly tell us how far they fall. Instead, the particle chooses the two rotations and their horizontal separation. A geometric calculation supplies the missing heights by placing the bodies in contact with what is below them. We first describe the coordinates it chooses, then the calculation that turns them into a scene.

The mug's horizontal centre of mass is already fixed by the table gauge. To locate the spoon, choose a distance and a direction from the mug. Let \(L=0.1\) m be a fixed length and let \(r\) be the distance in units of \(L\). If \(\varphi\) is the direction, the horizontal displacement vector is

$$v=\begin{pmatrix}rL\cos\varphi\\rL\sin\varphi\end{pmatrix},\qquad 0\leq r\leq r_{\max},\quad \varphi\in(-\pi,\pi].$$

Here \(\sin\) and \(\cos\) are the usual functions of an angle. The factors \(rL\) multiply their values: \(L\) is a constant, not a function. For example, \(r=0.5\) and \(\varphi=0\) put the spoon's centre of mass 50 mm along the horizontal x direction from the mug's. The bound \(r_{\max}L=20.2\) cm is the sum of the bodies' bounding radii, beyond which they cannot touch.

We also need to choose how the spoon is turned. We have already described its world rotation \(R_{\text{spoon}}\); it is useful to describe its orientation relative to the line joining the bodies. A turn through angle \(\varphi\) about the vertical is given by the matrix-valued function

$$R_z(\varphi)=\begin{pmatrix}\cos\varphi&-\sin\varphi&0\\\sin\varphi&\cos\varphi&0\\0&0&1\end{pmatrix}.$$

Multiplying a vector by \(R_z(\varphi)\) turns it through that angle while preserving its vertical component. Thus \(R_z(0)=I_3\), and \(R_z(\pi/2)\) turns the positive x direction into the positive y direction. Angles in these formulas are in radians. With this function defined, the spoon's rotation in the frame turned towards it is

$$Q=R_z(-\varphi)R_{\text{spoon}},\qquad R_{\text{spoon}}=R_z(\varphi)Q.$$

Keeping \(r\) and \(Q\) fixed while changing \(\varphi\) carries the spoon round the mug while preserving its attitude towards the joining line. The mug's own rotation remains \(R_{\text{mug}}\). Finally, a real coordinate \(\xi\) chooses which body is placed first: the spoon if \(\xi<0\), the mug otherwise. These choices together form the particle state:

$$x=(\xi,r,\varphi,R_{\text{mug}},Q),\qquad \xi\in\mathbb R,\quad R_{\text{mug}},Q\in SO(3).$$

The coordinates live in the lifted product space

$$\mathcal X=\mathbb R\times[0,r_{\max}]\times S^1\times SO(3)\times SO(3),$$

where \(S^1\) is the circle of directions. The first two factors contain the real order coordinate and the bounded radius; the third contains the periodic angle; the last two contain the mug rotation and the spoon's relative rotation. We will group the first three coordinates as \(u=(\xi,r,\varphi)\). Locally, \(u\) has three scalar coordinates, and each rotation factor has three tangent directions.

This is a space of particle coordinates, before the two heights are supplied. A geometric map \(T\) turns a particle into a physical scene \(s=T(x)\). The table gauge chooses representatives of the common-yaw freedom in this lifted space. There are also coordinate redundancies: only the sign of \(\xi\) affects placement order, and at \(r=0\) the polar direction is not unique. We will write the motion locally on the product factors and state the numerical rules at these seams separately.

2. Fornasier-Sun Polarised Consensus Based Optimisation

With the particle space specified, we can say what kind of motion we want on it. The reference is the polarised consensus model of Massimo Fornasier and Lukang Sun. First consider its Euclidean form. For particles \(z_i(t)\in\mathbb R^d\) and a nonnegative objective \(f:\mathbb R^d\to[0,\infty)\), its empirical particle equation is

$$dz_i=-\lambda(z_i-m_i)\,dt+\sigma\bigl(\|z_i-m_i\|+\epsilon_0\bigr)\,dB_i.$$

Here \(t\) is optimisation time, \(B_i\) are independent standard \(d\)-dimensional Brownian motions, \(\lambda>0\) sets attraction strength and \(\sigma\geq0\) sets diffusion strength. The nonnegative constant \(\epsilon_0\) is the paper's exploration floor, renamed here to distinguish it from the affinity parameter. The point \(m_i\) is a weighted consensus for the receiving particle \(i\): sources are favoured both for scoring well under \(f\) and for being near \(z_i\). Because those weights depend on \(i\), different parts of the population can follow different consensus points.

To define that consensus, Fornasier and Sun assign source \(z_j\) the affinity

$$A_f(z_j,z_i)=\frac{f(z_j)\bigl(f(z_i)+\vartheta\bigr)}{\varkappa} +\|z_i-z_j\|^2,\qquad \vartheta>0,\quad\varkappa>0.$$

The first term favours sources with a smaller objective, with a strength that depends on the receiving particle's objective. The second favours nearby sources. The parameter \(\varkappa\) sets their relative scale, and \(\vartheta\) supplies a positive offset. A positive inverse temperature \(\alpha\) then gives the weights and consensus point:

$$w_{ij}=\exp[-\alpha A_f(z_j,z_i)],\qquad m_i=\frac{\sum_{j=1}^Nw_{ij}z_j}{\sum_{j=1}^Nw_{ij}}.$$

The weighted mean can also be derived by holding these weights fixed and minimising their squared distances to a common point:

$$m_i=\operatorname*{arg\,min}_{m\in\mathbb R^d}\sum_jw_{ij}\|m-z_j\|^2, \qquad 0=2\sum_jw_{ij}(m_i-z_j).$$

Solving the last equality gives the displayed consensus formula. This is the Euclidean reference construction that we will apply to the scene problem.

The Euclidean equation supplies the reference structure: attraction towards consensus together with diffusion. In our scene problem, \(x_i\in\mathcal X\) replaces \(z_i\). A single arithmetic mean and ordinary subtraction cannot be used on every factor of \(\mathcal X\). We therefore need to construct a consensus separately for scalars, the angle and rotations, and use tangent directions for rotational motion.

The scene model also makes a declared diffusion change: it uses coordinatewise disagreement noise and a separate, score-dependent diffusion of strength \(\rho\), instead of the isotropic norm-plus-floor noise above. We derive that term after defining the measurements that drive it. First we need to turn each \(x_i\) into a scene and evaluate what happens when that scene is released.

3. Turning coordinates into a scene

At this point the rotations and horizontal positions are known, but the scene is still missing its two heights. Denote the horizontal centre-of-mass positions by \(v_{\text{mug}}=(0,0)\) and \(v_{\text{spoon}}=v\). For each body, let \(\mathcal B_b\) be its solid shape in local coordinates and \(q_b\) its local centre of mass. Placing that centre of mass at height \(h\) requires the translation

$$t_b(h)=\begin{pmatrix}v_{b,x}\\v_{b,y}\\h\end{pmatrix}-R_bq_b.$$

The subtraction accounts for a body-coordinate origin that need not coincide with its centre of mass. The occupied world shape at that height is then \(G_b(h)=\{R_bp+t_b(h):p\in\mathcal B_b\}\). To place the first body, find the lowest height at which it does not penetrate the table. To place the second, include the first body among its obstacles. Let \(\mathcal O_b\) denote the solid region occupied by these obstacles, including the table's half-space \(z\leq0\), and let \(\operatorname{int}\) denote the interior of a solid. Allowing the surfaces to touch while requiring the interiors to remain disjoint gives

$$h_b=\min\{h\in\mathbb R:\operatorname{int}G_b(h)\cap\operatorname{int}\mathcal O_b=\varnothing\},\qquad t_b=t_b(h_b).$$

For the first body, this simply puts its lowest point on the table, giving \(h_b=-\min_{p\in\mathcal B_b}[R_b(p-q_b)]_z\). For the second, the geometry routine finds the free intervals along its vertical line and takes the bottom of the lowest one. A spoon that fits inside or underneath the mug can therefore be placed there, rather than being stopped at an upper rim. The chosen rotations and horizontal positions stay fixed during this calculation.

Once the heights have been found, both poses are complete. We call the entire geometric construction \(T\):

$$T:x\longmapsto s=T(x)=\bigl((R_{\text{mug}},t_{\text{mug}}),(R_{\text{spoon}},t_{\text{spoon}})\bigr).$$

The particle is \(x\), and its physical scene is \(T(x)\). Computing this map uses the known shapes and geometric contact calculations. It does not advance a physics simulation or settle the bodies. A touching placement may still topple or slide; releasing it is how we find out.

4. Scene simulation

We now have a scene \(s=T(x)\) to test. Both bodies are given zero initial velocity and released for \(H=1\) second in MuJoCo, using the project's contact model and collider, friction 0.6 and a time step of \(\Delta\tau=2\) ms. During this release the bodies' poses change. Writing \(\tau\) for physical simulation time, their trajectory is

$$s_\tau=\bigl((R_b(\tau;s),t_b(\tau;s))\bigr)_b,\qquad s_0=s,\quad 0\leq\tau\leq H.$$

The first observation is where the scene ends. The function \(e\) returns the poses at the end of the release:

$$e(s)=s_H=\bigl((R_b(H;s),t_b(H;s))\bigr)_b.$$

These are endpoint poses; the bodies may still be moving at time \(H\). We also want to know how far they moved before reaching them, since a body could move away and return. For this, the observer follows a fixed set \(K_b\) of sampled material points on each body. The same pose-to-point relation from Section 1 now depends on time:

$$y_b(\tau,p;s)=R_b(\tau;s)p+t_b(\tau;s),\qquad p\in K_b.$$

The largest observed displacement of body \(b\) from its initial pose is

$$X_b(s)=\max_{\tau\in\mathcal T_X}\max_{p\in K_b}\|y_b(\tau,p;s)-y_b(0,p;s)\|,\qquad \mathcal T_X=\{0,\Delta\tau,2\Delta\tau,\ldots,H\}.$$

This is the greatest excursion from the starting position, rather than the accumulated length of a point's path. Because the observer uses finite point sets and time steps, it approximates the maximum over the full body and continuous release.

Motion is not the only quantity to monitor. The soft-contact simulation can also allow shapes to overlap. At each contact check, let \(\operatorname{depth}_{\rm contact}(s_\tau)\) be the greatest nonnegative penetration depth reported by the collision detector. Eligible pairs include shapes belonging to different bodies and a body against the table; separated shapes contribute zero. The peak reported overlap is

$$\delta(s)=\max_{\tau\in\mathcal T_c}\operatorname{depth}_{\rm contact}(s_\tau),$$

where \(\mathcal T_c\) denotes the contact checks during the numerical release, including its initial check. The starting placement also receives a separate geometric penetration check, denoted by

$$\delta_0(s)=\operatorname{depth}_{\rm geometry}(s).$$

Both depths have units of length. Together, the endpoint \(e(s)\), the excursions \(X_b(s)\) and these depths describe what happened to the scene when it was released.

5. A metric for comparing scenes

To use the release, we need a way to say how far the final scene is from the starting one. The same comparison will later let particles judge how similar their scenes are. A distance between body centres alone would miss rotations, so we compare corresponding material points instead.

For each body \(b\), choose a fixed set of points sampled from the surfaces of its geometric primitives, expressed in that body's local coordinates:

$$P_b=\{p_{b,1},\ldots,p_{b,n_b}\}\subset\mathbb R^3,\qquad |P_b|=n_b.$$

Thus \(P_{\text{mug}}\) samples the mug and \(P_{\text{spoon}}\) samples the spoon. These point sets are kept fixed across all scenes. They are the samples used for this distance; the observer's \(K_b\) in Section 4 is a separate sampling used to measure maximum motion.

Consider two scenes \(s\) and \(s'\), each written in the table gauge. The point \(p\) occupies the world positions \(y_b(p;s)=R_bp+t_b\) and \(y_b(p;s')=R'_bp+t'_b\). The unprimed poses come from \(s\), and the primed poses from \(s'\). Averaging the squared displacement over each body's points, then adding the two bodies' contributions, defines

$$\begin{aligned} d(s,s')^2 &=\sum_b\frac{1}{|P_b|}\sum_{p\in P_b}\|y_b(p;s)-y_b(p;s')\|^2\\ &=\sum_b\frac{1}{|P_b|}\sum_{p\in P_b}\|(R_bp+t_b)-(R'_bp+t'_b)\|^2. \end{aligned}$$

The distance \(d(s,s')\) is the square root of this sum and has units of length. It compares the same point in the two poses. A rotation therefore contributes according to how far it carries the body's material points, just as a translation does.

This average can be evaluated without transforming every sample point each time. The needed geometric information is the sample centroid \(a_b\) and covariance \(S_b\), defined by

$$a_b=\frac{1}{n_b}\sum_{p\in P_b}p,\qquad S_b=\frac{1}{n_b}\sum_{p\in P_b}(p-a_b)(p-a_b)^\top.$$

Let \(S_b^{1/2}\) be the positive semidefinite square root of this covariance. Writing \(\|\cdot\|_F^2\) for the sum of the squared matrix entries, the body's contribution to the squared distance is

$$\|R_ba_b+t_b-R'_ba_b-t'_b\|^2+\|(R_b-R'_b)S_b^{1/2}\|_F^2.$$

The identity represents each body by three centroid-position numbers and nine matrix entries. For the two-body scene this gives a 24-dimensional vector whose ordinary Euclidean distance is exactly the sampled distance \(d\).

6. Defining the objective function and scoring a scene

We can now measure how far a release carries its starting scene: it is \(d(s,e(s))\). To make excessive overlap costly as well, add the portions of the two measured depths that exceed the contact tolerances. With \((a)_+=\max(a,0)\), the objective assigned to particle \(x\) is

$$F(x)=d(s,e(s))+\eta\Bigl[(\delta(s)-0.4\ \text{mm})_++(\delta_0(s)-0.16\ \text{mm})_+\Bigr],\qquad s=T(x).$$

The depth limits allow numerical contact compression before adding a charge. The coefficient \(\eta\) is a dimensionless objective weight: each millimetre of excess depth contributes \(\eta\) millimetres to \(F\). It is separate from the physical friction coefficient. The value used here is

$$\eta=18.01710687513962\approx18.0.$$

The objective tells particles which scenes to favour. We also need a score that identifies scenes passing the finite at-rest test, for the gallery and for controlling extra exploration. This score uses the maximum excursion \(X_b\), so motion that reverses before the endpoint still counts. For particle \(j\), write \(s_j=T(x_j)\). Body \(b\)'s contribution beyond a tolerance \(\varepsilon=1\) mm is

$$C_{j,b}=\frac{(X_b(s_j)-\varepsilon)_+}{L},\qquad \varepsilon=1\ \text{mm},\quad L=100\ \text{mm}.$$

The overlap contribution is the same charge as in \(F\), divided by \(L\):

$$\begin{aligned} C_j^{\text{overlap}}=\frac{\eta}{L}\Bigl[&(\delta(s_j)-0.4\ \text{mm})_+\\ &+(\delta_0(s_j)-0.16\ \text{mm})_+\Bigr]. \end{aligned}$$

Adding these contributions defines the dimensionless rest score \(C_j\):

$$C_j=C_{j,\text{mug}}+C_{j,\text{spoon}}+C_j^{\text{overlap}}.$$

Every contribution is nonnegative. Thus \(C_j=0\) precisely when both maximum observed displacements are at most 1 mm and both overlap limits are met. A positive value measures the excess. For example, a spoon excursion of 3 mm, with the mug within tolerance and no overlap charge, gives \(C_j=(3-1)/100=0.02\).

The two scores have different jobs: \(F(x_j)\), measured in units of length, supplies the consensus weights; \(C_j\), which is dimensionless, is the gallery's “energy” and controls the added diffusion in Section 8. Passing the rest test does not require \(F=0\), because the objective continues to measure endpoint displacement below 1 mm. A scene is called static when it also stays within the same excursion tolerance in ten-second releases at both 2 ms and 1 ms time steps. These remain finite numerical tests.

7. Choosing a polarised consensus point

Suppose the population contains \(N\) particle states \(x_1,\ldots,x_N\). Each has a decoded scene \(s_j=T(x_j)\), a released endpoint \(e(s_j)\) and an objective value \(F_j=F(x_j)\). A particle will be attracted towards a weighted mean of other particle states. To choose those weights, it needs to consider both how well another scene scores and how close that scene is.

The scene metric alone is not the full distance used here. Two placements can start close together but release into different scenes; alternatively, distant placements can end in the same place. We compare both starts and endpoints:

$$D_{ij}^2=d(s_i,s_j)^2+d(e(s_i),e(s_j))^2.$$

For \(D_{ij}\) to be small, both terms must be small. This gives a neighbourhood based on the placements and their release behaviour, with \(D_{ij}\) still measured in units of length.

We now apply the affinity defined in Section 2. Take \(f=F/L\), \(1/\varkappa=L^2\), replace the Euclidean distance by \(D_{ij}\), and choose \(\vartheta=1\). This gives the scene affinity

$$A_{ij}=F_j(F_i+\vartheta L)+D_{ij}^2.$$

Smaller \(A_{ij}\) means a more attractive source. A positive inverse-temperature parameter \(\alpha\) converts these affinities into weights:

$$w_{ij}=\exp(-\alpha A_{ij}).$$

The weights depend on the receiving particle \(i\). The population can therefore have different consensus points rather than all particles sharing one mean. The comparison with a particle's own affinity makes the tradeoff explicit. Since \(D_{ii}=0\), particle \(j\) receives more weight than \(i\) gives itself exactly when

$$A_{ij}\lt A_{ii}\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad D_{ij}^2\lt(F_i-F_j)(F_i+\vartheta L).$$

A source must therefore improve the objective enough to justify its distance. Because \(F_j\geq0\), a necessary condition is \(D_{ij}^2\lt F_i(F_i+\vartheta L)\). The length \(\vartheta L=0.1\) m controls how far this preference for better sources can reach.

The Euclidean consensus in Section 2 minimises a weighted sum of squared distances. On our product space, choose a sum of such distances, one appropriate to each factor. With the same weights used throughout, that minimisation separates into a mean on each factor.

For the real order coordinate and the radius, ordinary squared distance gives

$$\bar\xi_i=\frac{\sum_jw_{ij}\xi_j}{\sum_jw_{ij}},\qquad \bar r_i=\frac{\sum_jw_{ij}r_j}{\sum_jw_{ij}}.$$

The radius mean remains in \([0,r_{\max}]\) because it is a convex combination of admissible radii. For the angle, averaging angle values would depend on where the circle is cut. Instead, represent a direction by the unit-vector function \(\gamma(\phi)=(\cos\phi,\sin\phi)\) and minimise the weighted squared chord distance \(\sum_jw_{ij}\|\gamma(\phi)-\gamma(\varphi_j)\|^2\). Expanding the squares leaves the maximisation of \(\sum_jw_{ij}\cos(\phi-\varphi_j)\), giving

$$\bar\varphi_i=\operatorname{atan2}\!\left(\sum_jw_{ij}\sin\varphi_j,\ \sum_jw_{ij}\cos\varphi_j\right).$$

The function \(\operatorname{atan2}(y,x)\) returns the direction of the planar vector \((x,y)\). This circular mean is unique when the weighted direction vector is nonzero; if it vanishes, the minimisation has no preferred direction and the implementation's angle convention supplies a representative.

For each rotation factor, use squared Frobenius distance between rotation matrices. For example, minimising \(\sum_jw_{ij}\|M-R_{j,\text{mug}}\|_F^2\) over \(M\in SO(3)\) is equivalent to finding the closest rotation to the weighted matrix mean. Denote this closest-rotation operation by \(\operatorname{Proj}_{SO(3)}\). The two factor means are therefore

$$\begin{aligned} M_{i,\text{mug}}&=\operatorname{Proj}_{SO(3)}\!\left(\frac{\sum_jw_{ij}R_{j,\text{mug}}}{\sum_jw_{ij}}\right),\\ M_{i,\text{spoon}}&=\operatorname{Proj}_{SO(3)}\!\left(\frac{\sum_jw_{ij}Q_j}{\sum_jw_{ij}}\right). \end{aligned}$$

These are chordal rotation means, rather than means defined by squared rotation-log distance. If a matrix mean has a nonunique closest rotation, the numerical projection chooses one. The spoon block averages the relative rotations \(Q_j\), because that is the factor searched by the particle. Together the factor means give

$$m_i=(\bar\xi_i,\bar r_i,\bar\varphi_i,M_{i,\text{mug}},M_{i,\text{spoon}}).$$

This point lies in the lifted product \(\mathcal X\). It is then expressed in the same table gauge as the particles; we use the same symbols for that representative. Thus the affinity compares physical scenes and their releases, while the averaging takes place factor by factor in the particle coordinates. It is not a claim that this coordinate consensus minimises the physical scene distance \(d\), or that its decoded scene must itself pass the rest test.

It remains to choose how sharply \(\alpha\) favours the smaller affinities. Since \(A_{ij}\) has units of squared length, \(\alpha\) has units of inverse squared length. Specify a Gaussian width \(\ell\) for the distance factor by requiring

$$\exp(-\alpha D_{ij}^2)=\exp\!\left(-\frac{D_{ij}^2}{2\ell^2}\right).$$

Matching the exponents gives the fixed setting used in this formulation:

$$\alpha=\frac{1}{2\ell^2},\qquad \ell=0.16\ \text{mm},\qquad \alpha=19\,531\,250\ \text{m}^{-2}.$$

The width is the project's inherited numerical contact-resolution scale, motivated by soft-contact compression. It is a modelling choice, not a value fixed by a convergence theorem or selected by a fresh Q13 parameter sweep. The same \(\alpha\) multiplies the objective part of the affinity, so the full weight is

$$w_{ij}=\exp\!\left[-\frac{F_j(F_i+\vartheta L)}{2\ell^2}\right]\exp\!\left[-\frac{D_{ij}^2}{2\ell^2}\right].$$

This setting stays fixed throughout a run, without annealing or an effective-sample-size adjustment.

8. Keeping exploration active

The reference model's disagreement noise vanishes when a particle equals its consensus, unless its exploration floor is positive. Here we instead want the added diffusion to depend on how far the weighted source scenes are from passing the finite rest test. Average their measured scores using the consensus weights:

$$\bar C_i=\frac{\sum_jw_{ij}C_j}{\sum_jw_{ij}},\qquad \bar C_{i,b}=\frac{\sum_jw_{ij}C_{j,b}}{\sum_jw_{ij}}.$$

These are averages of source scores. They need not equal the score obtained by decoding and releasing the consensus itself. The total average, including overlap, will drive exploration in \(u=(\xi,r,\varphi)\); each body's motion average will drive exploration in its rotation factor.

Write \(c\geq0\) for whichever average applies to the factor under consideration. Choose the bounded response

$$\varsigma(c)=\frac{c}{1+c}.$$

This response is zero when the average score is zero, positive otherwise, linear near zero and less than one. Those properties motivate the choice, but do not determine it uniquely. We now derive the diffusion amplitude from a stated generator on a factor's three tangent directions.

For a smooth test function \(\psi\), let \(\mathcal D_n\psi\) denote differentiation in a unit tangent direction \(n\in S^2\). In the local scalar coordinates, \(\mathcal D_n\psi=n\cdot\nabla\psi\). On a rotation factor, let \(\widehat n\) be the skew matrix satisfying \(\widehat n\,z=n\times z\); then

$$\mathcal D_n\psi(U)=\left.\frac{d}{d\epsilon}\psi\bigl(U\exp(\epsilon\widehat n)\bigr)\right|_{\epsilon=0}.$$

A diffusion generator gives the instantaneous expected rate of change of a test function. Our modelling assumption is to average scalar diffusion over uniformly distributed tangent directions, with strength \(\rho^2\varsigma(c)^2\):

$$\mathcal L_{\rho,c}\psi =\rho^2\varsigma(c)^2\int_{S^2}\mathcal D_n^2\psi\,\frac{d\Omega(n)}{4\pi}.$$

Here \(d\Omega/(4\pi)\) is uniform probability on the unit sphere, and the score coefficient is evaluated at the current state, outside the directional derivatives. The three components of a uniform direction have equal second moments; because their squares sum to one,

$$\int_{S^2}nn^\top\,\frac{d\Omega(n)}{4\pi}=\frac13I_3,\qquad \mathcal L_{\rho,c}\psi=\frac{\rho^2\varsigma(c)^2}{3}\sum_{k=1}^3\mathcal D_k^2\psi.$$

Independent Brownian increments of amplitude \(a(c)\) in those three directions have generator \(\tfrac12a(c)^2\sum_k\mathcal D_k^2\). Matching the two generators therefore gives

$$\frac12a(c)^2=\frac{\rho^2\varsigma(c)^2}{3} \quad\Longrightarrow\quad a(c)=\rho\sqrt{\frac23}\,\frac{c}{1+c}.$$

Thus the factor \(\sqrt{2/3}\) follows from the direction-averaged generator and the Brownian generator's factor \(1/2\). The generator itself is a model choice, rather than a consequence forced by PCBO.

For our factors, the resulting amplitudes are

$$a_i^u=\rho\sqrt{\frac23}\,\varsigma(\bar C_i),\qquad a_{i,b}=\rho\sqrt{\frac23}\,\varsigma(\bar C_{i,b}).$$

The parameter \(\rho\geq0\) sets the strength of the added diffusion. This independent, score-dependent diffusion is a project extension of the reference equation. Its directional symmetry refers to the chosen dimensionless coordinate block and the body-frame rotation coordinates.

9. The stochastic dynamics on the search space

We have now specified the product space, the factor consensus points and the added diffusion. We can write the actual scene dynamics. Let \(U_{i,\text{mug}}=R_{i,\text{mug}}\). For the spoon, write \(Q_{i,\text{spoon}}=Q_i\) to identify its relative-rotation coordinate explicitly, and set \(U_{i,\text{spoon}}=Q_{i,\text{spoon}}\). Optimisation time is \(t\), distinct from the physical release time \(\tau\). The attraction rate is one, and the coordinatewise disagreement-noise coefficient is \(\sigma=1.3095\).

First express each particle's disagreement with its consensus on each factor. For the coordinate block, let \(\bar u_i=(\bar\xi_i,\bar r_i,\bar\varphi_i)\). Its disagreement vector is

$$e_i^u=\bigl(\xi_i-\bar\xi_i,\ r_i-\bar r_i,\ \operatorname{wrap}(\varphi_i-\bar\varphi_i)\bigr).$$

The function \(\operatorname{wrap}\) chooses the angle in \((-\pi,\pi]\). On a rotation factor, the relative rotation \(U_{i,b}^{\top}M_{i,b}\) takes the current frame towards its consensus. The skew-matrix map \(\omega\mapsto\widehat\omega\) was defined above; its inverse is denoted by \(\vee\). Taking the principal matrix logarithm gives the local tangent vector

$$\omega_{i,b}=\log(U_{i,b}^{\top}M_{i,b})^\vee,\qquad b\in\{\text{mug},\text{spoon}\}.$$

Let \(e_1,e_2,e_3\) be the standard basis vectors and put \(H_k=\widehat e_k\). The amplitudes \(a_i^u\) and \(a_{i,b}\) were derived in Section 8. The variance in rotation direction \(k\) is

$$\nu_{i,b,k}=\sigma^2\omega_{i,b,k}^2+a_{i,b}^2.$$

Let \(W_i^u,B_i^u\) be standard three-dimensional Brownian motions, and let \(W_{i,b,k},B_{i,b,k}\) be standard scalar Brownian motions. These driving motions are independent across particles, factors and the two noise terms. The three local Itô SDEs are written together below, followed by the algebraic relation giving the spoon's world rotation. The equations use the lifted coordinates, before restoring the common-yaw table gauge:

$$\begin{aligned} \substack{\text{coordinate factors}\\\mathbb R\times(0,r_{\max})\times S^1}:\quad du_i={}&-e_i^u\,dt+\sigma\operatorname{diag}(e_i^u)\,dW_i^u+a_i^u\,dB_i^u,\\[1.2em] \substack{\text{mug}\\SO(3)}:\quad dR_{i,\text{mug}}={}&R_{i,\text{mug}}\left[\widehat\omega_{i,\text{mug}}+\frac12\sum_{k=1}^3\nu_{i,\text{mug},k}H_k^2\right]dt\\ &+\sigma\sum_{k=1}^3\omega_{i,\text{mug},k}R_{i,\text{mug}}H_k\,dW_{i,\text{mug},k} +a_{i,\text{mug}}\sum_{k=1}^3R_{i,\text{mug}}H_k\,dB_{i,\text{mug},k},\\[1.2em] \substack{\text{spoon (relative)}\\SO(3)}:\quad dQ_{i,\text{spoon}}={}&Q_{i,\text{spoon}}\left[\widehat\omega_{i,\text{spoon}}+\frac12\sum_{k=1}^3\nu_{i,\text{spoon},k}H_k^2\right]dt\\ &+\sigma\sum_{k=1}^3\omega_{i,\text{spoon},k}Q_{i,\text{spoon}}H_k\,dW_{i,\text{spoon},k} +a_{i,\text{spoon}}\sum_{k=1}^3Q_{i,\text{spoon}}H_k\,dB_{i,\text{spoon},k},\\[1.2em] \substack{\text{spoon (world)}\\SO(3)}:\quad R_{i,\text{spoon}}={}&R_z(\varphi_i)Q_{i,\text{spoon}}. \end{aligned}$$

The final line computes the spoon's world rotation from its relative rotation and direction. The first SDE also moves the spoon horizontally through \(r_i,\varphi_i\), and \(T\) supplies both bodies' heights from the resulting coordinates.

In the first equation, \(\operatorname{diag}(e_i^u)\) puts the three disagreement components on a diagonal, so each drives its own multiplicative noise. The first two components have the usual Euclidean SDE structure; the third is the corresponding local equation on the circle. The vector \(e_i^u\) points away from consensus, while each \(\omega_{i,b}\) points towards it, accounting for the negative coordinate drift and positive rotational drift.

The two rotation equations preserve \(SO(3)\). Their symmetric \(H_k^2\) drift is the Itô curvature correction: because \(H_k^\top=-H_k\), it cancels the quadratic variation in \(d(U_{i,b}^\top U_{i,b})\). A continuous solution that starts orthogonal with determinant one retains both properties.

These are local equations on the interiors of the coordinate domains, away from the rotation-log half-turn cut and the polar and order seams. The numerical treatment of those seams and the discretisation of the SDEs are recorded in Appendix A.6.

10. Starting the population

The preceding sections describe the motion of an existing population. To start it, draw the placement order by a fair coin, draw both world rotations uniformly over \(SO(3)\), and draw the spoon's horizontal offset uniformly in the interaction disc. Uniformity of the rotations means that no orientation is preferred; for the disc, uniform area corresponds to \(r=r_{\max}\sqrt{U}\), with \(U\) uniform on \([0,1]\), and an independent uniform direction \(\varphi\).

One part of these draws is then prepared before the search begins. The body placed first is released alone on the table, with one-second releases repeated until its maximum observed excursion is below 1 mm, for at most twenty releases. This preparation uses simulation to obtain candidate resting postures for the initial population. It is performed once, separately from the geometric map \(T\) used at every evaluation.

To give the different candidate postures comparable representation, group them before assigning them back to particles. Two settled rotations are linked when, with a common turn about the vertical ignored, they differ by less than the angle corresponding to 1 cm at the body's bounding radius, capped at one radian. A connected group of these links defines a posture. Before grouping, each candidate is disturbed about a random horizontal axis by that angle and released alone again; it is retained for the groups only if it was quiet before and after, and returns within the angle. The angles for these bodies are 7.3° for the mug and 4.7° for the spoon.

The particles placing a given body first are divided as evenly as their integer count allows among its posture groups, then draw a settled rotation from their assigned group. The second body's random rotation and the horizontal-offset draws are kept. Both rotations are expressed in the table gauge, and \(Q\) is computed from the resulting spoon rotation and direction as in Section 1. All postures come from the run's own single-body releases. Once this starting preparation is complete, both bodies remain free in the joint particle dynamics.

11. Result 1 - The cost landscape

The landscape and gallery below show the run on seed 12; the appendix also gives seed 11.

The dropdown below selects a family. Each picture is then a slice through one scene of that family which the run found and which is static for ten seconds, the calmest one. Two coordinates of the particle are changed on a grid and all others are held; every grid point is turned into a scene by the map \(T\) and released exactly as a particle would be, and the height is its objective \(F\) in millimetres. Cells at rest are green. The dot marks the scene itself and is drawn on top of the surface, also where a wall of the surface stands in front of it; turning the picture shows what lies behind. Three pairs of coordinates are shown side by side: the direction \(\varphi\) and the distance between the bodies; two turns of the spoon; two turns of the mug. The close-up covers ±60° and ±60 mm around the scene. The whole range covers every direction, every turn and every distance at which the bodies can touch, and is the same picture over the larger domain. Dragging turns the three pictures together.

The run holds no scene of three families. For all of them the slice goes through a scene of the family that was found in an earlier experiment and is static for ten seconds there, written in the coordinates of this formulation; the line under the pictures says which run it comes from.

The scene the slices go through, from the side and from above. Click to turn it.

Range Top of the height scale
at rest

Three things can be read off these surfaces. The first is that the objective is graded around every scene. Turning the spoon or the mug away from the scene by 1.5°, 3°, 6°, 12° and 24° raises it to 2.8, 6.7, 19, 35 and 65 mm at the median over the seventeen families that the solver holds, the two bodies, the two axes and both senses, which is about 3 mm per degree over the first six degrees. A particle some ten degrees away from a scene at rest is told which way to turn.

The second is that the set at rest is wide in some directions and thin in others, and this is what separates the families that are easy to hold from those that are hard. With the spoon lying on the table apart from the upright mug, the whole close-up in direction and distance is at rest, and so is 86 % of the whole range; with the spoon resting on the upside-down mug the shares are 69 % and 90 %. With the spoon inside the upright mug, 5 of the 6561 cells of the same close-up are at rest. They lie on a thin line, which is bent because \(\varphi\) is measured about the centre of mass of the mug, and the handle pulls that off the axis of the cup. On the inner side of the line the objective rises by about a millimetre per millimetre; on the outer side it jumps to between 19 and 34 mm within 3 mm. Over the inside of the mug the objective falls from a median of 27 mm near the centre to 10 mm near the wall, because a spoon lowered anywhere inside falls against the wall. On the rim the median is about 80 to 120 mm, and outside the mug the objective is 202 mm everywhere: the spoon topples onto the table, which is a travel of 130 mm and an overlap charge of 72 mm for the impact. For this family the landscape is a basin whose floor, one to three centimetres high, tells a particle that it is inside the mug, with a narrow slot in the floor.

The third is the cliffs. A spoon leaning on the mug on its side keeps the objective below 10 mm everywhere within 6° and 6 mm of the scene; a little further out it falls off the mug and the objective jumps to between 100 and 200 mm. The surface beyond a cliff says nothing about the scene on the near side of it.

13. What it does not do

It does not find every family. Three of the 20 known families are not held: Mug on its side, spoon propped steeply on the mug (7 starting scenes fall into it; 32 % of its scenes stay in the family under the 3° disturbance); Mug tilted, spoon inside the mug (no starting scene falls into it; 75 % of its scenes stay in the family under the 3° disturbance); Mug upright, spoon propped steeply on the mug (3 starting scenes fall into it; 83 % of its scenes stay in the family under the 3° disturbance). The number of starting scenes that fall into a family does not decide alone whether it is held: Mug upright, spoon inside the mug is held from 3 of them, while Mug on its side, spoon propped steeply on the mug is lost from 7. No family was reached that no starting scene falls into.

It finishes slowly. After 250 updates 6318 of the 10 000 particles are at rest and 8326 are within 2 mm of rest, while 1856 are alone within their reach, not at rest, and move only by the additive noise. A variant with the same search space, in which the body put down first also starts at rest but without equal shares for its postures, and with the largest displacement of any point as the objective, the distance taken between the scenes alone, the wide reach and no additive noise, ends 150 updates on the same seed with 8006 static scenes in 14 families, without the spoon inside the upright mug.

It treats one body specially, and it has only been run on two bodies. The body put down first starts at rest and the polar coordinates are taken about the mug; the control run of Appendix A.4 shows that these carry part of the result. The objective and material-point distance can be extended by summing over more bodies, and the particle weights need not enumerate every contact graph. That observation does not establish scalable search: a release becomes more expensive as bodies and contacts are added, and the number of distinct resting families can grow. The present two-body starting law, relative coordinates and geometric placement map have not been extended and tested for arbitrary scenes.

Appendix: results and numerical details

Both runs of 250 updates: seed 12, the run of the body of the page, and seed 11. Twenty families are known for this mug and spoon, namely those of which some search has produced a scene that passes the ten-second static test; they are the yardstick for a run.

A.1 Particles at rest

of 10 000, against the update

The curve counts particles. The tiles above, the gallery and the table of A.3 are taken on the consensus points of the last update, which are what a run returns and what the ten-second check is run on; the two counts at rest differ by a few dozen.

A.2 Particles with the spoon inside the upright mug

of 10 000, against the update, at rest or not

A particle is counted when its spoon is inside an upright mug, at rest or not. On seed 12 the count rises from 3 at the start to at most 24 and ends at 22; on seed 11 it rises from 2 to 19 by update 21 and ends at 9. The static consensus scenes of the family at the end are 19 on seed 12 and 1 on seed 11 (3 and 1 distinct). In arm Q6 of the same morning (first body at rest and polar coordinates as here, but the largest excursion as the objective, the distance taken between the scenes alone, the wide reach and no additive noise), the count on seed 12 rose to 16 by update 12, was 4 at update 40, and stayed at zero from update 88 on (objective study, section 10.4).

A.3 The families

Families are named from the contacts of the scene; they are coarse descriptions, not proved components. Robustness: up to 60 static scenes of the family, taken from all runs of the study, were each disturbed four times (both bodies turned by 3° about a random axis and shifted by 3 mm, then put back down) and released for ten seconds; the column gives the share that ends in the same family. Starting scenes: how many of the 10 000 starting scenes are taken into the family by their first release. Distinct: static scenes that are pairwise further apart than about 5 mm or 3°, counted up to 60. Names marked “not tested” occur only as the end of a first release or among particles that are not at rest; no run of the study holds a static scene of them, and they are not counted among the twenty. A finite disturbance test is not a proof of stability.

A.4 The same formulation with no body treated specially

A control run shows what the starting law of Section 10 and the polar coordinates contribute. In it both bodies start with random rotations and the offset is kept in plain coordinates; objective, distance, weights and noise are the same. It ends with 4728 and 4847 static scenes in 11 and 12 families. On both seeds it has no static scene with the spoon inside the upright mug (0 and 0, against 1 and 19 here), none with the spoon leaning on the upright mug (0 and 0 against 4 and 12), and of the tilted-mug families only 0 and 3 scenes of the spoon lying apart (against 85 and 80). It keeps the spoon inside the mug on its side (57 and 21 static). The two things were changed together, so their separate shares are not measured.

A.5 Measurements behind the formulation

Geometry and initialisation. The lowering map takes 0.03 s for 10 000 particles, measured alone. Of the 10 000 starting scenes on seed 12, 3 pass the at-rest test. Preparing the first-body postures takes 18 s once. Released alone, the mug ends on its side in 72 % of the cases, upside down in 14 %, upright in 14 %, and tilted onto rim and handle once in about five thousand. The preparation gives the mug 10 postures with about 509 particles each and the spoon 2 with about 2454 each. With both bodies initially random, earlier measurements showed that spoon exploration had already contracted before the mug came to rest; this motivated the prepared first-body rotations.

Overlap and objective. On seed 12, the overlap charge is positive for 6682 of the 10 000 starting scenes. Among these scenes its median share of \(F\) is 13 %. After 250 updates it is positive for 56 particles. It is zero for every scene counted as at rest. At the end of the run, four fifths of the scenes at rest have \(F\) between 0.2 and 0.8 mm. Earlier objectives based on the maximum excursion overemphasised the sweep of a long spoon, while subtracting the rest tolerance inside the objective left particles near that tolerance.

Distance between particles. With distance taken between initial scenes alone, a particle with the spoon inside the upright mug and not at rest followed a scene outside the mug in 93 % of 2091 cases (seed 12, mug given upright, first 30 updates), at a median distance of 2.5 cm. The family ended empty. Using end scenes alone also admitted followers whose initial scenes were 8 to 10 cm apart and could tilt a resting mug towards one still falling. These observations motivated using both initial and end scenes.

Extra noise and reach. In a run with \(\vartheta=0\) and without extra noise, 8982 of 10 000 particles ended as their own consensus points without passing the at-rest test; 34 were at rest (mug given upright, seed 12, 100 updates). With the additive noise on, the same probe left 1328 particles at rest for \(\vartheta=0\), 6750 for \(\vartheta L=0.1\) m and 9422 for the wide reach. The wide reach removed the spoon-inside-upright-mug family in a joint seed-12 run. The chosen intermediate reach is an empirical setting; these comparisons do not establish a universal value.

A.6 Numerical realisation of the dynamics

The coordinate SDE is stepped with Euler–Maruyama at \(\Delta t=0.1\). For a rotation, take independent standard normal vectors \(z,z'\in\mathbb R^3\) and evaluate its coefficients at the start of the step:

$$\begin{aligned} \zeta_{i,b}&=\omega_{i,b}\Delta t+\sigma\sqrt{\Delta t}\,\omega_{i,b}\odot z+a_{i,b}\sqrt{\Delta t}\,z',\\ U_{i,b}^{n+1}&=U_{i,b}^n\exp(\widehat\zeta_{i,b}). \end{aligned}$$

The exponential turns a skew matrix into a rotation, keeping the updated matrix in \(SO(3)\). It also accounts for the curvature drift in the Itô SDE: expanding the exponential gives

$$\mathbb E\!\left[\tfrac12\widehat\zeta_{i,b}^{\,2}\mid\text{current state}\right] =\tfrac12\Delta t\sum_{k=1}^3\nu_{i,b,k}H_k^2+O(\Delta t^2).$$

The implementation therefore obtains this correction through the exponential itself. This is the local Itô interpretation of the pre-step scheme; an uncorrected Stratonovich equation with state-dependent coefficients would be a different model. Malham and Wiese discuss exponential methods for keeping stochastic iterates on Lie groups.

After the step, the scene is expressed in the table gauge and decoded through \(T\). The numerical boundary rules map a negative radius to \(r\leftarrow|r|\), \(\varphi\leftarrow\varphi+\pi\), and clip a radius above \(r_{\max}\) to that bound. The angle is periodic; after decoding, the order coordinate is recorded by its sign as \(\xi=\pm1\). These rules supplement the interior SDEs at their boundaries and seams, where no global smooth SDE is asserted. Every moved particle's new scene then receives a release evaluation, ready to form the scores and consensus for the next update.

The added-diffusion coefficient was introduced historically as \(\sqrt{2/D}\), then applied with \(D=3\) per block. Section 8 reconstructs an equivalent direction-averaged generator for that choice.
